title: Inbox/deduplication pattern
description: Learn the inbox pattern for idempotent message processing. Understand how to handle duplicate messages reliably by tracking processed messages.

data.text: The inbox pattern provides idempotency for message consumers by tracking processed messages in an inbox table. This ensures that duplicate messages don't cause incorrect state changes.
With at-least-once delivery, consumers must handle duplicates. Without deduplication, duplicates can cause incorrect state.

items: Message retries cause duplicate processing
Consumer crashes after processing but before ack
Network failures cause redelivery
Non-idempotent operations fail on duplicates
Data corruption from repeated operations

data.title: Assume Duplicates
data.text: Design consumers assuming duplicates will occur. The inbox pattern makes handling duplicates safe and explicit.
The inbox pattern stores processed message IDs in a table to detect and skip duplicates.

items: Before processing, check if message ID exists in inbox
If exists, skip processing—already handled
If not exists, process the message
Insert message ID into inbox after successful processing
Use a transaction to ensure atomicity

data.title: Key Benefit
data.text: The inbox pattern provides explicit deduplication that's easy to understand and debug. Unlike hidden idempotency, it's visible in the data model.

items.title: Separate Inbox Table
items.description: Dedicated table for tracking processed message IDs. Simple, clear separation. Requires additional query per message.

items.title: Inbox Column on Business Table
items.description: Add processed_message_ids column to business tables. Fewer queries but pollutes business schema.

items.title: Unique Constraint on Message ID
items.description: Use database unique constraint for deduplication. Atomic, efficient. Requires message ID in business data.

items.title: Redis-based Deduplication
items.description: Use Redis for fast deduplication checks. High performance, but not durable like database inbox.

items: Use a unique constraint on message ID for atomic deduplication
Include message metadata (timestamp, payload hash) in inbox
Set TTL on inbox entries to prevent unbounded growth
Monitor inbox size and cleanup old entries
Use the same transaction for inbox insert and business logic
Consider batch processing for efficiency

data.text: Inbox tables grow without bound. Implement cleanup to prevent database bloat.

items: Time-based cleanup—delete entries older than N days
Size-based cleanup—delete oldest entries when table exceeds size
TTL on inbox entries—automatic expiration if supported
Archive old entries—move to cold storage for audit
Partition by time—easier cleanup of old partitions

data.title: Cleanup Trade-off
data.text: Aggressive cleanup saves space but may lose deduplication for very old duplicate messages. Choose TTL based on your message redelivery window.
Use the inbox pattern when you need explicit, reliable deduplication.

items: When message delivery is at-least-once
When operations are not naturally idempotent
When you need audit trail of processed messages
When duplicates would cause serious problems
When you want visible, debuggable deduplication
Pros: Explicit deduplication, easy to debug, works with any message system
Cons: Additional database writes, storage overhead, cleanup complexity
Performance: Extra query per message can impact throughput
Complexity: Requires careful transaction handling
